memoryAid: One single horizontal stroke stands for ‘one’. It's about as simple as a symbol gets. Stack two strokes and you get 二 (two), stack three and you get 三 (three).
女 is a simple stick drawing of a woman, sometimes pictured sitting with her legs crossed. On its own it means ‘woman,’ and now and then ‘daughter.’
人 is a simple stick figure of a person: two strokes are the legs, planted apart as someone stands or walks. Don't confuse it with 入 ‘enter’, which looks almost the same.
十 is just a plain cross, a horizontal 一 cut by a vertical 丨. It's an arbitrary sign chosen to mean ‘ten,’ so picture the cross as a tally mark for 10.
囗 is a closed box, a border drawn all the way around, so it means ‘to surround.’ It's the old form of 围 (to go around), and it shows up as the outer frame in over 20 modern characters.
田 is a drawing of a field seen from above. The outer frame is the whole field, and the cross inside marks the raised paths that split it into small rice paddies.
力 is a drawing of a plow, and pushing a plow through the soil takes real strength. Be careful not to mix it up with 刀 (knife), which looks very similar.
Picture 力 (strength) put to work under 田 (field). In old times, the one who used muscle to plow the fields was the man, so 男 means ‘male.’

丨 is simply one vertical line, so it's the ‘downstroke.’ It used to be read gǔn, but today everyone calls it shù (the vertical stroke). You won't see it standing alone as a word. It shows up as the radical in a handful of common characters.
亻 is the narrow form 人 (person) takes when it sits on the left side of a character. It never appears alone, but it's a key radical, and in some characters it points specifically to a man.
乙 is one twisting stroke. In early writings it meant the guts of a fish, and it may once have been a drawing of them. Today it means ‘second,’ as the 2nd heavenly stem.
艺 first meant the skill of gardening, which is why 艹 (grass) sits on top. Below it, 乙 gives the sound. Picture tending plants as the first art or craft.

忄 is the squeezed side form of 心 (heart), and it only shows up inside other characters, never alone. In Chinese thought the heart and mind count as a single thing, so 忄 in a character often points to feelings or thinking.
忄 (heart) carries the meaning: what you remember stays in your heart. 乙 (twist) hints at the sound yì.

女 (woman) marks this as ‘she,’ and 也 once hinted at the sound, though it doesn't match well now. The character is a fairly recent coinage, made under the influence of European languages that split pronouns by gender.
他 ‘he’ pairs 亻 (person), which gives the meaning, with 也, which once hinted at the sound. It's a man's character, so it has the person radical. Compare 她 ‘she’, which uses 女 (woman) instead.
门 is a picture of a gate. The older full form 門 looks like a pair of swinging saloon doors, one on each side, so it means ‘gate, door, entrance.’
亻 (person) shows that 们 pluralizes words for people, like 我们 ‘we’. 门 (gate, mén) gives the sound.
手 shows a hand with its fingers spread out. When it sits on the left side of another character, it usually shrinks to 扌 (hand), which counts as its own radical.
扌 is the side form of 手 ‘hand’. It never stands alone as a character and only shows up as a part of other characters. Don't mix it up with 才 ‘then’ or 寸 ‘thumb’.
弋 is a picture of a dart, an arrow with a string tied on so the hunter can pull it back after shooting. Picture shooting at prey and reeling in your catch.
戈 is a picture of an ancient weapon, sometimes called a dagger-ax. It looks like 弋 (dart) with one extra stroke at the bottom, and that stroke is the blade the real weapon had at its lower end.
我 started out as the name of a lance-like weapon, built from 扌 (hand) and 戈 (lance). It came to mean ‘I, me’ only because it sounded like that word. Picture yourself as the one holding the lance.
亠 looks like a little lid with a knob on top: a dot 丶 sitting on a flat line 一. Its older, broader sense is anything that sits on top of something else and covers it.

土 looks like a cross planted in the ground, which makes it easy to remember as ‘earth, soil’ (that's only a visual trick, not its real origin). Its bottom line is the longer one, like wide ground. In 士 ‘knight’ the bottom line is shorter.
Think of 士 as 十 (ten) above 一 (one): a knight or scholar who takes ten things and organizes them into one for his lord. 士 means scholar, gentleman, or soldier.

冖 is a cloth draped over the top of something, so it means ‘cover.’ Imagine it as a crown sitting on a head. You won't see it standing alone; it only shows up on top of other characters. It has no dot, which sets it apart from 宀 (roof).
小 started out as three tiny dots meaning ‘small.’ The two outer dots are still there, and the middle one has turned into a hooked downstroke 亅.

尔 got its meaning ‘you’ by borrowing: the character was used for the word because they sounded alike, and the look has nothing to do with the meaning. It has a formal, literary feel, like an old-fashioned ‘thou.’
尔 already meant ‘you’ all by itself. Adding 亻 (person) makes it obvious that the word points to a person, and the result is 你, ‘you.’
宀 is a picture of a roof. Think of the dot 丶 on top as a chimney sitting on the covering 冖 below. It's the roof over more than 50 common characters.
它 started as a picture of a cobra. Over time the drawing got distorted into 宀 (roof) on top of 匕 (ladle). Its sound was later borrowed for the word ‘it; other.’
子 is a drawing of a baby: a head on top, arms spread wide along the stroke 一, and legs wrapped up tight below. Picture a swaddled infant waving its arms and you have ‘child’.
A 女 (woman) next to her 子 (child) is a picture of well-being and something everyone wants, so 好 means ‘good.’

厶 started out as a drawing of a nose. People in China often point at their own nose to mean ‘me,’ so the shape came to stand for what's yours alone: private, or selfish. It's the early form of 私 ‘private.’
幺 started out as a drawing of a small coil of silk thread. A thin little twist of thread is a good picture for its meaning, ‘tiny, small.’

纟 is the slim form of the silk radical, a twisted strand of thread, and it sits on the side of a character. When silk goes at the bottom of a character, it usually takes its fuller form 糸 instead, likely because that looks better.
Men worked the 田 (field) and women raised silk for 糸 (thread). With both jobs piling up, everyone gets tired. It first meant ‘to pile up,’ and ‘tired’ came later.

彳 started as a picture of a crossroads, but its modern shape is garbled. Try reading it as 亻 (person) with an extra stroke that shows a step being taken. It shows up often in characters about moving or doing.
艮 started out as a drawing of a man with one huge, glaring eye. Picture a stubborn guy staring you down: he's as blunt and tough as chewy, leathery food.
很 first meant ‘to be stubborn, resist’: 艮 (stubborn) carries that idea, and 彳 (step) was added to make it clearer. Later the character was borrowed to write hěn, ‘very.’
口 is a simple drawing of an open mouth: a square opening. Besides ‘mouth,’ it also works as a measure word for counting people.

灬 shows flames flickering along the ground, and you only see it inside other characters. In the traditional forms of animal words like ‘horse,’ ‘bird,’ and ‘fish,’ the same four dots are really stylized legs or tails and have nothing to do with fire.

马 is a picture of a horse. The traditional 馬 shows it more clearly, with four dots along the bottom. In the simplified form those dots shrink to a single stroke 一, like a horse in such a hurry its legs blur together.
口 (mouth) tells you 吗 is something spoken, and 马 (horse) is only there for its sound, ma. Put 吗 at the end of a sentence and the sentence becomes a question.
At the bottom of 言 sits 口 ‘mouth’. Picture the lines stacked on top as words streaming out of it, or as the mouth moving while it talks. That's speech.
讠 is the short form of 言 ‘words,’ used on the left side of many characters. When you see it, expect the meaning to involve speaking or language.
隹 began as a simple drawing of a bird. It usually means a short-tailed bird, and some old texts use it for a dove. Today you mostly see it as a part inside other characters, not as a word of its own.
To ask ‘who?’ you use words, so 讠 (speech) gives the meaning. 隹 (zhuī) hints at the sound shéi/shuí.
大 shows a person standing with arms stretched wide, making himself as big as he can. Put it with its opposite 小 (small) and you get 大小, ‘size’, literally ‘the big and the small of it’.
夫 is a grown man 大 with an extra stroke 一 across his head, which stands for a hairpin. He's the adult man of the house: a husband.
天 looks like a person 大 with a big head, a god in human form. The line 一 across the top stands for the heavens above that figure, so the character means ‘sky, heaven’.
气 shows breath drifting away in wavy layers, like the curls of steam you can see coming off a hot drink. That's why it means air, gas, or vapor.
竹 shows two bamboo stalks with their thin leaves hanging down. When it sits on top of other characters it gets squashed into a slightly different shape, and it marks words for things made of bamboo.
Imagine ⺮ (bamboo) in the wind above 夭, a person bending. The bamboo sways and leans back the way someone tips back when they laugh.

儿 is the short form of 兒, which pictures a child whose skull still has its soft spot open. Picture the two strokes 丿 and 乚 as little legs running around. Long ago this shape was known as the ‘legs’ component.
尢 shows two legs where one is shorter than the other, so the figure is ‘lame.’ The horizontal stroke across the top makes the uneven leg lengths stand out.
Picture having to stand 立 (stand) for ten 十 (ten) hours straight. That is bitter, exhausting work.

王 is often read as three strokes for heaven, humans and earth, with the king as the line joining them. The oldest oracle-bone forms tell a different story, though: they show an axe, the weapon that backs up a king's power.
Picture three jade disks (the horizontal strokes) threaded on one cord (the vertical stroke). The extra 丶 dot probably marks it as jade, so it isn't mistaken for 王 ‘king’.
A dot 丶 sits on top of 王 ‘king’, and a king is a lord or master, which is what 主 means. 主 also gives its zhǔ sound to several common characters, like 住 and 注.
A person 亻 stays put somewhere, so 住 means to live or stay. 主 (zhǔ) on the right gives the sound zhù. After a verb, 住 means brought to a stop or stumped.
氵 is the side form of 水 (water). It never appears as a character by itself, but you'll see it in many characters for liquids. Imagine its three dots as splashing drops.
氵 (water) points to the sense ‘to pour into,’ and 主 gives the sound zhù. Think of pouring all your attention into one spot, and you get ‘to concentrate.’
驻 first meant a horse coming to a stop. 马 (horse) gives the meaning and 主 (zhǔ) gives the sound zhù. Now it means to stop or be stationed somewhere.

木 is a drawing of a tree: a trunk with branches spreading at the top and roots at the bottom. As a component it often shows up in names of wooden objects, and on its own it can also mean stiff or ‘wooden’.
禾 looks like 木 (tree) with one extra slanting stroke 丿 across the top. That stroke is the heavy, ripe head of grain drooping from the stalk.
矢 is a drawing of an arrow standing upright. Its tip is at the top, and the fletching and notched end are at the bottom.
The top of 亡 was once 人 (person) or 入 (enter): someone ducking into a corner to hide. The first meaning was ‘to flee, to hide,’ and ‘be gone’ and ‘to die’ came from it.
When you're this busy, your 忄 (heart) just wants to run off and 亡 ‘flee’. 亡 (wáng) also hints at the sound máng.

心 began as a drawing of a heart, and you can still spot the heart shape in its old form. It works as a character by itself, and it also turns up as a part at the bottom of other characters, where it brings the sense of heart or feeling.
您 puts 你 ‘you’ on top of 心 ‘heart’. It's the respectful ‘you’, said with heart when you speak to elders or superiors.
儿 (legs) at the bottom stands for a person, and 二 on top marks his head. The head comes first and matters most, so 元 means ‘first’ or ‘origin’. It also stands in for 圆, so it can mean ‘dollar’.
辶 started as a drawing of a foot stopped at a crossroads. It never appears as a character by itself, only as a part of other characters, and in those it usually has to do with walking and moving.
云 started as a drawing of a cloud, and ‘cloud’ is its first meaning. It also means ‘to say’ because it sounds the same as an old word for ‘say’ and was borrowed to write it.
辶 (walk) stands for movement, which fits ‘to transport,’ and 云 (cloud) gives the sound yùn. Picture goods drifting along the road like clouds.

阝 looks like an ear but has nothing to do with hearing. Its position tells you the meaning: on the right side of a character it means ‘city’, and on the left it means ‘mound’, drawn as steps leading down from a hill.
A garden or park is a space with a wall around it, which is what the enclosure 囗 shows. Inside sits 元, and it gives the sound yuán.
太 began as the same word as 大 ‘big’. Add one dot 丶 and ‘big’ becomes ‘extremely’ or ‘too much’.
高 is a drawing of a tall building: 亠 is the roof on top, and the 口 ‘mouth’ and 冋 shapes stacked underneath are its windows and storeys. A tower like that stands high, so 高 means ‘tall’ or ‘high’.
又 is a sketch of a right hand. It came to mean ‘again’ only because the word sounded the same, so the hand picture was borrowed to write it.
攴 ‘to knock, to hit’ gives 敲 its meaning of rapping or striking. 高 (gāo, ‘tall’) hints at the sound qiāo.
稿 also means a grain stalk, which is why 禾 (grain) is on the left. 高 (gāo, ‘tall’) gives the sound gǎo. Today it mostly means a draft or manuscript.

月 is a drawing of the moon, and by itself it means ‘moon’ (and ‘month’). As a component, watch out: the old ‘moon’ and ‘meat’ radicals looked the same and are now one form, so inside other characters 月 can stand for 肉 (meat).
Under 高 (gāo, ‘tall’), which gives the sound, sits ⺼ ‘meat’, which gives the meaning: 膏 is the fat and grease from meat, and by extension an ointment or paste.
阿 first meant ‘slope’: 阝 (mound) points to the hillside, and 可 (kě) gives the sound. Its job today as a prefix for names comes only from borrowing that sound.
阿 was borrowed for the ‘ah’ sound. Later 口 ‘mouth’ was added to show it's a spoken exclamation you say at the end of a sentence.
肀 is the upper part of 聿, which began as a drawing of a hand gripping a Chinese writing brush. Read 彐 as the hand and the stroke 丨 through it as the brush it holds.
曰 is a 口 ‘mouth’ with a stroke 一 inside, maybe the tongue moving as you speak. Unlike 日 ‘sun’, it's shorter and wider, and the inner stroke usually doesn't reach the right side.

书 started out as a writing brush above 曰 (say), meaning words put down with a brush. That gives writing, and from it books, letters and documents. Today's simplified form hardly shows the brush anymore.
卩 ‘seal’ nearly always sits on the right side of a character, the same spot where 阝 (right ear) goes, so take care not to mix the two up. You'll rarely see 卩 on its own.

Picture 卩 as a man kneeling in shackles, with a hand, 扌 and 又, handing out his punishment. That's payback, the original meaning. The senses ‘report’ and ‘newspaper’ were later borrowed because they share the same sound.
毛 is a drawing of an animal's pelt, with strands of fur fanning out, so it means hair, fur, or feathers. It looks a lot like 手 ‘hand’, so don't mix them up.
A classic Chinese writing brush has a bamboo handle and a tip made of hair. So 笔 puts ⺮ (bamboo) over 毛 (hair) to show a brush, or any pen.
Here 王 stands for 玉 ‘jade’, and toys were often carved from jade. Add 元 (yuán) for the sound and you get 玩 (wán), to play with something.
钅 is the squeezed side version of 金 (gold, metal). It never stands alone, but it shows up in over 200 characters, often ones naming metals or things made of metal.
山 is a drawing of a mountain range. Its three upward strokes are three peaks, and the old forms show them even more clearly. On its own it means ‘mountain’ or ‘hill.’

冈 means ‘ridge’. Its older form 岡 held 山 (mountain) inside, which fits a hill's crest. The simplified form swaps that for a plain 乂 ‘X’ under 冂, so picture a ridge line crossing over a mountain you can no longer see.
Steel is a metal, so 钢 has 钅 (metal) on the left. On the right, 冈 (gāng, ‘ridge’) gives the sound gāng.

纟 (silk thread) points to the meaning, since 纲 is the main rope of a net, possibly first a silk rope. 冈 gives the sound gāng. Pull that main rope and the whole net follows, which is why 纲 also means a guiding principle or an outline.
铅 means lead, the heavy metal. The 钅 (metal) on the left tells you it names a metal.
米 began as a drawing of rice plants growing in a paddy. One reading says the horizontal stroke is the water standing in the field. Don't mix it up with 木 (tree) or 禾 (grain).
A riddle is made of words 讠 that get you lost 迷 (to be confused or lost). 迷 also gives the sound mí.
目 (eye) on the left tells you this is about eyes, like squinting or getting dust in them. 米 (rice) on the right gives the sound mī.
刀 began as a simple drawing of a knife. Don't confuse it with 力 (strength), which looks very similar.

Look at the top, 八: it shows something split into two halves, and under it sits 刀 (knife), the tool doing the cutting. A knife splitting a thing apart gives you ‘to divide,’ and the pieces are fractions or shares.
Face powder was once made from rice, so 米 (rice) gives the meaning ‘powder.’ 分 (fēn) supplies the sound.
Picture silk threads 纟 (silk) coming apart and tangling into a confused mess. 分 (fēn) gives the sound.
目 (eye) tells you this is about looking, gazing and hoping for something. 分 (fēn) hints at the sound pàn, though the match isn't exact.
皿 is a picture of a bowl seen from the side, with its flat base along the bottom. Picture a dish or container ready to be filled.
贝 pictures a cowrie, a small glossy shell that served as money in ancient China. That's why 贝 shows up in characters about value, money, and trade.
Put 分 (divide) over 贝 (cowrie shell, money): once your money gets split up again and again, very little is left, so you're poor.
气 (breath, vapors) gives the meaning of air hanging around you, the atmosphere. 分 (fēn) tucked underneath gives the sound fēn.
Fields 田 sitting on land 土 make a village 里. Its other meanings, like the distance unit and ‘inside,’ are borrowed for their sound.
理 first meant the veins in jade, so 王 on the left ties to jade here, and 里 gives the sound lǐ. Think of the grain in a piece of jade when you see 理.
口 (mouth) on the side tells you to read this for its sound only, and 里 gives that sound, lī. It spells out spoken sounds like 哩哩啦啦 ‘off and on’ and foreign words like 啫哩 (jelly).
Picture a little one who stands (立) inside the village (里). That's 童, a child.
A single stroke 丨 goes straight down through the middle of the box 口, so 中 means ‘middle’ or ‘center.’ Think of an arrow hitting a target dead center.
A bell or clock is a metal object, so 钅 (metal) marks the meaning, and 中 (zhōng, ‘middle’) gives the sound.
衣 is a drawing of a gown, and in older forms you can clearly see the sleeves and the skirt. When it shows up as a part of another character, it often points to something you wear.
表 puts 毛 (fur) over 衣 (clothing), like a fur overcoat. An overcoat is the layer everyone sees, so the word for ‘outer coat’ and the sense ‘to show, on the outside’ likely come from the same root.
羊 is a picture of a sheep. The two strokes on top, shaped like 丷 (eight), are its horns, and the lines under them make up the head and body.
美 puts 羊 (sheep) on top of 大 (big). A big, plump sheep is a fine and pleasing sight, so the pair means ‘beautiful.’
夕 is a sketch of the moon. When the moon shows up in the sky, it's dusk and evening is coming. Don't mix it up with 歹, which looks similar.
卜 shows the crack in a heated tortoise shell. Ancient Shang kings had diviners heat shells until they split, then read the cracks to tell the future. That's why 卜 means ‘to divine.’
外 joins 夕 (dusk) with 卜 (divination). In divination, the telling crack shows up on the outer surface of the tortoise shell, so the character means ‘outside.’
A hand 手 (slightly squashed on top) rests over an eye 目, like shading your eyes to get a better look. That's why it means ‘to look at.’

西 started out as a drawing of a bird's nest and meant ‘to nest.’ It came to mean ‘west’ only because it was borrowed for a word that sounded the same. At the top of other characters it acts as a ‘cover’ radical, since reformers grouped it with a similar-looking cover form.

贝 (cowrie shell, once used as money) sits at the bottom, so the character has to do with money: expensive, precious. The top part isn't used as a character on its own anymore, but it gives the sound guì.
礻 is the side form of 示 ‘sign, to show’, as in signs sent from heaven, so it marks things to do with spirits. Don't mix it up with 衤 (clothing), which has one extra dot on the right.
且 pictures a tablet or altar for honoring ancestors, and it first meant ‘ancestor.’ Today it's borrowed for its sound to mean ‘moreover.’ In other characters it often gives the sound zu or cu.
In the old days, rent was charged on farmland and paid with harvested grain. That's why 租 (rent) has 禾 (grain) on its left.
纟 (silk thread) gives the meaning: you gather threads together to build something, the way you form a group. 且 gives the sound zǔ.
米 (rice) points to the meaning: grain that hasn't been finely milled is coarse. 且 on the right gives the sound, cū.
阝 (mound) hints at the meaning: a mound of earth in your way blocks the path. 且 gives the sound zǔ.

宜 began as a picture of a sacred altar pole with meat hung on it, and it meant an offering to the earth god. Its sound was later borrowed for ‘fitting, proper.’ You can picture 且 (the altar) under 宀 (roof), where everything is set out properly.
罒 is a drawing of a net: an outer frame with mesh lines stretched across it. You don't see it as a character on its own. It shows up only as a part, and it always sits on top of the character.
Think of 大 as a person standing with arms spread. The two dots ⺀ point at the top of that figure, and the top of a person is the head.
买 (to buy) is a shortened, stylized form of its traditional character. The traditional form combined an eye with cowrie shells, which served as money, so both parts point to the meaning.
卖 is 买 (buy) with 十 (ten) on top. Picture buying things and then selling ten of them: that's why 卖 means ‘to sell.’
耂 is a shortened form of 老 ‘old’, which pictures an old man with long hair leaning on a cane. When you see 耂 at the top of a character, expect a meaning about age or seniority.
Think of 者 as Chinese ‘-er’: put it after a verb and you get the person who does that action. 者 also gives its sound to several other characters, so learning it now makes them easier later.

犭 is the side form of 犬 ‘dog’, so it sits on the left of characters. It turns up in names of mid-sized animals like wolves, monkeys and cats, and in words about beastly traits such as ferocity, cruelty and courage.
犭 (animal) tells you this is a creature, and 者 (zhě) hints at the sound zhū. Together they make an animal called zhū: the pig.
To boil something you need heat, so 灬 (fire) sits at the bottom and gives the meaning. 者 on top gives the sound, zhǔ.
日 (sun) sits on top, bringing the summer heat, and 者 below hints at the sound shǔ.
纟 (silk) gives the meaning: 绪 is the loose end of a thread. Pull on it and you find a clue, or where a line of thought begins. 者 on the right gives the sound.
Picture a wall of packed 土 (earth) blocking the way. That's 堵: a wall, or to stop something up. 者 on the right gives the sound.
A government office is like a 罒 (net) that ties many workers together, and 者 (zhě) underneath gives the sound shǔ.
阝 (city) on the right gives the meaning ‘metropolis, capital’, and 者 once gave the sound. The common meaning ‘all’ comes from borrowing the character for its sound.
廾 is drawn as a pair of hands joined together, as if clasped. It mostly shows up as a part inside other characters, not as a word of its own. Don't mix it up with 艹 ‘grass’ or 廿.
廿 is just two 十 ‘ten’ joined into one shape, and two tens make twenty. When you read it aloud, you usually just say 二十 èrshí.
Picture 廿 as an open mouth, and the short line 一 inside it as a bit of something sweet you're tasting. A mouth holding a treat means ‘sweet’.
或 first meant ‘nation’: 戈 (lance) for its army, 口 (mouth) for its language, and 一, which began as ‘earth,’ for its land. It came to mean ‘or’ and ‘perhaps’ only because it was borrowed for its sound.
匚 is a drawing of a basket or box lying on its side, with its open mouth facing right. These days you see it only as a part inside other characters, not as a word by itself.
五 means ‘five.’ Picture 王 (king) knocked sideways and leaning on a walking stick. You can also read it as a crossing mark set between two lines, 一 for heaven above and 一 for earth below.
The 木 (wood) at the bottom hints that this is something made of wood, like a table. To remember its shape, read it from top to bottom as 卜 (divine), 日 (sun), and 木 (wood).
大 (big) sits on top of 可 (able, can). Picture something huge that can do anything. That's strange and uncanny!
A chair is traditionally made of wood, so 椅 has 木 (tree/wood) on the left for meaning. 奇 (qí) on the right gives the sound.

东 started out as a drawing of a tied-up bundle. It came to mean ‘east’ only because the word sounded the same. People later read the older form 東 as the sun 日 caught in a tree 木 at sunrise. That isn't the real origin, but it's still a handy picture for remembering ‘east.’
戋 was first drawn as two 戈 (lance) stacked together, a picture of ferocity that meant ‘fierce, cruel.’ Its meaning ‘thin, small’ is only borrowed for the sound.
钅 (metal, gold) points to money, and 戋 (jiān) hints at the sound qián. Coins are made of metal.
浅 pairs 氵 (water) with 戋, which gives the sound and may also carry a sense of ‘thin’. A thin layer of water is shallow.
文 began as a picture of a person with a pattern marked on the chest, most likely a tattoo. Patterns you can ‘read’ on skin led to its meanings of writing, literature and culture.
The top 亼 once meant ‘come together,’ and below it sits 口 (mouth). Think of lips closing, or two halves of a double door swinging shut. That's 合: to join or bring together.
Picture a hand grabbing a chunk of meat, drawn here as 月 (meat). If you're holding meat, you're well off, so the character means ‘to have.’
干 began as a picture of a shield, and a shield fits the idea of ‘to oppose.’ Its other meanings, like ‘dry’ and ‘to do,’ were borrowed because the words sounded alike.
A pole is cut from a tree, so 木 (tree, wood) gives the meaning. 干 (gān) supplies the sound.

走 started out as a person on top of a foot 止, and the person's shape later got worn down into 土. It first meant ‘to run,’ and in the south, including Cantonese, it can still mean that. Today it usually means ‘to walk.’
To hurry after someone, you need 走 (walk/run), which carries the meaning. 干 (gān) sits inside it and gives the sound gǎn.
厂 started as a drawing of a slope or cliff face. When characters were simplified it took over the meaning ‘factory,’ so now you can picture a workshop built against the side of a cliff.
A 山 (mountain) sits over a 厂 (cliff or slope), which pictures a high, steep bank at the water's edge: the shore. 干 (gān) is a sound hint, but it only gives the rhyme of àn.
日 (sun) sits on top and shows the meaning: hot sun that dries the land into drought. 干 underneath gives the sound, hàn.
刂 is the form 刀 ‘knife’ takes when it sits on the right side of a character. It never stands on its own. It only turns up as a part of other characters.
刂 (knife) shows the carving, and 干 gives the sound kān. Printing was once done from carved woodblocks, so to carve came to mean ‘to publish.’
殳 is a picture of a hand, 又 ‘right hand’, gripping a club, 几, ready to strike. Think of it as ‘club’ or ‘to club’. These days it rarely stands alone as a character.
没 has 氵 (water), which suits its meaning of flooding or sinking under water, and 殳 gives the sound. The same sound is also borrowed to say ‘not,’ so 没 negates 有 ‘to have’ and other verbs.
身 is drawn as a person whose torso is the biggest, most noticeable part. Some read it as a pregnant woman with a round belly. It can also mean ‘self.’
寸 shows a hand, and its little dot marks the thumb. A thumb's width is about an inch, so 寸 means ‘inch’, and by extension anything small.
身 now looks like ‘body,’ but it began as a drawing of an arrow set on a bow. 寸 (hand) is pulling the bowstring back, so together they mean to shoot.

Think of 士 (scholar or knight) standing over 口 (mouth): when a learned person speaks, it brings good fortune, so 吉 means ‘lucky.’ The real origin is different, but this old reading makes it easy to remember.
桔 is the everyday form of 橘 ‘tangerine’: 木 (tree) marks the fruit tree, and 吉 hints at the sound. In 桔汁 (júzhī) it simply means orange juice.
The top, 壴, started out as a picture of a drum, and 口 ‘mouth’ sits under it. Put drumming and singing together and you get a good time, so 喜 means to enjoy or be happy.
The bottom of 欠 is 人 (person). Think of the ⺈ on top as that person's hand held over the mouth mid-yawn. The character means ‘yawn’, and also ‘to owe, to lack’.
欠 (yawn) carries the meaning of 欢, happy, perhaps as a mouth opened wide to smile or laugh. 又 ‘right hand’ is a later stand-in for the part that used to give the sound.
止 started as a drawing of a foot. It once stood for things feet do, both marching and halting, but only ‘to stop’ is still used today. Picture a foot planted firmly on the ground.
足 is a picture of a foot. The 口 on top stands for the leg, and the shape underneath it is the ‘toe’ element. That toe shape shows up clearly when 足 appears as part of other characters.
The bottom of 青 looks like 月 ‘moon.’ Imagine the landscape under the moon glowing in nature's colors: green, sky blue, even a greenish black.
情 pairs 忄 (heart) with 青 (qīng), which gives the sound. It's a heart matter pronounced qíng, so it means emotion or feeling.
Water 氵 that looks 青 (blue-green, azure) is clear water. 青 also gives the sound qīng.
When the 日 (sun) shines in a 青 (blue) sky, the weather is clear and fine. 青 (qīng) also gives the sound qíng.
Put 目 (eye) next to 青 (azure, blue-green) and you get the pupil of the eye. 青 (qīng) also gives the sound, jīng.
Picture a 口 (mouth) poking through a 门 (door) to ask someone questions. 口 gives the meaning, and 门 (mén) used to give the sound.
An 耳 ‘ear’ sits inside 门 (door), which suggests the sound wén. Picture an ear at the door, listening in to hear the news.
Picture a log of 木 (wood/tree) wedged across your 门 (door) so nobody can bother you. Behind that barricade you can finally enjoy some idle time.
A knife, 刂, slices beside 另 ‘another’, cutting things apart so each goes its separate way. That's why 别 means to separate or to part, and also ‘other’.
朋 began as a drawing of two matching strings of shells hanging side by side. Picture the two 月 as that identical pair: two things that match and belong together, the way friends do.
友 puts a left hand together with a right hand 又 to mean ‘friend.’ Think of the old farewell gesture: you clasp your own two hands in front of you and bow to a friend.
毋 (don't!) is said to picture a woman in chains. Picture her restrained and unable to act. It looks a lot like 母 (mother), so check the difference carefully.
Picture a person on 儿 (legs) with a huge eye on top. The traditional form 見 draws that eye as 目, so the whole character is a person looking, which is why it means ‘to see.’
亲 names the hazel tree. Picture a tree 木 with fruit 立 on top. In the older way of writing ‘relatives; hold dear,’ 亲 was the part that gave the sound, so it came to stand for that word too.
母 shows a woman, and its two dots mark her breasts, which is how you know it means ‘mother.’ Look for those two dots: 毋 ‘don't’ has a single stroke through the middle in their place.
Picture an arrow 丨 held back on the bow 弓 and never fired: holding back like that is an act of mercy, so 弔 means ‘to pity.’ Today people usually write 吊 instead.
女 (woman) tells you the meaning, and 且 (qiě) gives the sound jiě. Put them together and you get a woman in the family: your elder sister.

长 began as a drawing of a man with a long beard. Now it's just a loose sketch of him. Picture those long whiskers for ‘long,’ and remember that a man with a beard that long is older, which fits ‘senior’ and ‘to grow.’
Think of 田 (field) as open countryside, framed inside 凵 with 一 across the top, like a landscape painting on an easel. That makes 画 ‘picture’ or ‘to paint.’
臼 is a picture of a mortar, the bowl you grind things into powder in. Its split shape sets it apart from 白 ‘white’, 日 ‘sun’ and 曰 ‘say’.
勹 is a drawing of a wrapper curling around something. When it shows up inside other characters, it usually curves around the other pieces, wrapping them up just like its meaning says.
Picture 勹 (wrapping) curled around 巳 (a baby), like swaddling, and you have 包 ‘wrap’. It also lends its sound, bao or pao, to many common characters.
A hug means your 扌 (hand) goes around someone and 包 (wrap) closes them in. 包 also gives the sound, bào.
Picture 包 ‘wrap’ next to ⺼ (flesh): a wrapping of flesh around the baby, which is the placenta or womb. 包 also gives the sound bāo.
衤 is the squeezed side form of 衣 (clothing). It always sits on the left of a character, and the characters that contain it usually have to do with clothes. On its own, the word is written 衣.
A robe is clothing, 衤 ‘clothing’, that wraps, 包 ‘wrap’, all the way around you. 包 (bāo) also hints at the sound páo.
Picture 氵 (water) wrapped up inside 包 ‘wrap’ and you get a bubble. 包 also gives the sound pào.
饣 is the squeezed-down form of 食 ‘food’ that sits on the left side of a character. Wherever you see it, the character has to do with food or eating.
饣 (food) plus 包 ‘wrap’: think of having so much food that it wraps you up. You're full! 包 (bāo) also hints at the sound bǎo.
火 is a drawing of a fire. The center stroke shoots up like a tall tongue of flame, and the small strokes on each side are sparks flying out.
巳 started as a picture of an unborn baby, with a big head on top and a curled-up body underneath. Picture that tiny curled shape as the sixth earthly branch, which also names the hours from 9 to 11.

巴 started out as a drawing of a boa, a snake big enough to swallow an elephant. Later it was borrowed for its sound to mean ‘open hand,’ and from there ‘to stick to’ and ‘to hope for.’ Picture a snake coiled tight around the thing it wants.
父 ‘father’ sits on top and gives the meaning, and 巴 underneath gives the sound bà. Imagine a boa (巴) coiled at Papa's feet.
本 is 木 (tree) with an extra line across its base that marks the roots. The root is where a tree starts, so 本 means ‘root, origin, basis.’
Farmers used to pay their taxes in grain. So 禾 (grain) next to 兑 ‘hand over’ means tax: grain you hand over to the state.
讠 (speech) gives the meaning ‘to speak,’ and 兑 (duì) gives a rough hint of the sound. In older texts, 说 sometimes stands in for 悦 ‘delighted.’
Imagine a story handed down through 十 (ten) generations of 口 (mouths). Anything retold that many times must be ancient. 古 also shows up as a sound part in other characters.
攵 shows a hand gripping a weapon, ready to strike, which is why it means ‘to rap’ or ‘to tap.’ Don't confuse it with 夂, 文, 殳, or 支, which look alike.
古 (old, ancient) gives the sound gù. Add 攵 (tap, strike) and you get the idea of turning something into a thing of the past, which fits senses like ‘ancient’ and ‘to die.’
A 亻 (person) does the estimating, and 古 (gū, ‘old’) gives the sound: gū, to appraise or estimate.
A 木 (tree) that is 古 (ancient) has dried out and withered with age. 古 (gǔ) also gives the sound kū.
古 (old, gǔ) on top gives the sound gū, and 辛 ‘bitter’ below points to the meaning. Think of a bitter old past that hides a crime.
重 may have started as a picture of a weighing scale, which fits its meaning ‘heavy.’ To remember its parts, think of a load carried 千 (a thousand) 里 (miles). It gets heavier with every step.
Picture a foreman directing workers who haul 重 (heavy) loads of 艹 (grass). 重 also hints at the sound, dǒng.
懂 is 董 (dǒng) with 忄 ‘heart/mind’ added on the left. To understand is to get something right in your mind, and 董 still gives the sound dǒng.
先 shows a foot 止 stepping out in front of a person 儿, so it means ‘first’ or ‘ahead’. Picture: the top looks like half a cow, standing on the two legs of 儿.
Picture a plum as the child of a tree: 子 (child) sits under 木 (tree), so 李 means ‘plum.’ It's also a very common surname.
亥 started out as a drawing of a wild boar, and it still looks a lot like 豕 (pig). Today it names the 12th earthly branch. As a part of other characters it often gives the sound hai, or sometimes gai.
孩 means child. 子 (child) gives the meaning and 亥 (hài) gives the sound. Picture 亥 as a pig with its little one 子 beside it: every piglet is somebody's child.
子 (child) at the bottom is the student. The top part once showed one hand guiding another as it learns to write, so the whole character means to study or learn.
Under the evening moon 夕 you can't see who's out there, so you use your 口 ‘mouth’ to call out a name.
Picture a 子 (child) sitting under the 宀 (roof) at home and practicing written characters. 子 also gives 字 its sound, zì.
牛 began as a picture of a cow seen head-on, with its horns sticking up at the top. Look for that horn stroke poking through the top, because 午 (noon) has no horn and looks almost the same.
Picture 牛 (cow) above 口 (mouth): a muzzle strapped over a cow's mouth. Or imagine shouting a warning that a bull is charging. Either way, the 口 is telling someone something, so 告 means ‘to inform.’
斤 started out as a drawing of an axe, so picture a blade on a handle. Today it's also a unit of weight, the jin or catty.
知 puts 矢 (arrow) beside 口 (mouth). When you really know something, your words fly out quick and straight to the target, like an arrow.
首 started as a drawing of a head, with 丷 as the hair or antlers on top of 自. A chief is the person at the head of a clan, so the same character means both ‘head’ and ‘leader’.
此 was first drawn as 止 (toe, foot) next to 匕 (a person). A person's feet mark the spot where they stand, so the character means ‘this’ place, right here.
枝 is 支 with 木 ‘tree’ added to make its sense clear: a branch of a tree. 支 also gives the sound zhī.
英 first meant ‘flower, to bloom’: 艹 (grass, plants) on top gives the meaning, and 央 (yāng) below hints at the sound yīng. The sense ‘bold, heroic’ came later, borrowed for its sound.
黑 first meant the soot or charcoal that builds up in a chimney over the fire 灬, and soot is black. That's how it came to mean ‘black’ and ‘dark’.

占 puts ⺊ (divination crack) over 口 (mouth): a diviner reads the cracks and speaks their meaning out loud, so the character means ‘to divine.’ Its other senses, like ‘seize,’ come from borrowing its sound.
立 (stand) gives the meaning and 占 (zhān) gives the sound. Think of a bus stop or taxi stand, a place where people stand and wait.
Imagine sticky cooked 米 (rice) clinging to your fingers: that's the meaning, ‘to paste, sticky.’ 占 (zhàn) on the right gives the sound zhān.
戈 (a spear/lance) stands for fighting, so 战 means war or battle, and 占 (zhàn) supplies the sound.

广 is a drawing of a lean-to: a roof with a dot on top, which is why it can mean ‘building’. Today it mostly stands in as the simplified form of 廣 guǎng, ‘broad, wide’. Keep it apart from 厂 ‘slope’ and 疒 ‘sickness’.
A shop sits under 广 (a lean-to building), and 占 (zhàn) sits inside it to suggest the sound diàn. Think of a little store tucked under a roof.
钅 (metal) marks this as a metal tool, a drill that bores through things. 占 gives the sound. It also means ‘diamond’.

零 first meant a single drop of water: 雨 (rain) on top gives the meaning, and 令 (lìng) gives the sound. Picture one raindrop, just a tiny bit and almost nothing, and then shrink it all the way to zero.
页 started as a picture of a person's head, and ‘head’ was its old meaning, which is no longer used. Today it means a page or leaf of a book.
The bottom of 齿 is a picture of an open mouth 凵 with teeth 人 inside it. On top, 止 (zhǐ) hints at the sound chǐ.
Teeth reveal how old someone is, so 齿 ‘teeth’ gives 龄 its meaning of age, and 令 (líng) gives the sound.
邻 means ‘neighbor’: 阝 (town) on the right points to cities sitting next to each other, and 令 hints at the sound lín.
Pity is something you feel in the heart, so 怜 has 忄 (heart) on the left. The 令 on the right tells you the sound, lián.

A single vertical stroke cuts straight down through 丷 (eight) and the two flat 一 strokes, slicing everything into halves. Funny twist: 半 looks like a cow with both horns, while 牛 ‘cow’ shows just one horn, like half a cow.
多 ‘many’ gives the meaning: once you have many, you have enough. 句 (jù) used to hint at the sound.
Picture 大 ‘big’ as a person putting on an archer's thimble and getting ready to draw the bow. You'll mostly see 夬 as a sound part, giving jue or kuai in several characters.
Think of a clod of 土 (earth) as a lump or chunk, and 夬 (kuài) tells you how to say it. A chunk can also be a dollar: 一块钱.
Picture a carpenter putting his 目 (eye) up close to a piece of 木 (wood) to check it. At first 相 meant ‘to examine,’ and it's now used for ‘each other’ and ‘appearance.’
相 on top gives the sound xiǎng, and 心 (heart) below stands for the mind. Picture looking something over inside your mind: that's thinking.
Early forms of 共 show the hand-clasp shape 廾 twice, so lots of hands join in. Everyone pitches in, which gives the meaning ‘all together, jointly’.
Picture a 亻 (person) beside 共 (together, or both hands held out): people gather to worship and offer up gifts, so the character means to offer or supply. 共 also gives the sound gōng.
氵 (water) on the left tells you this is about a huge amount of water, a flood. 共 gives the sound hóng, which some hear as the roar of rushing floodwater.

京 is a drawing of a tall building: 亠 is the roof, 口 the main hall, and 小 its supports. It first meant ‘tall building,’ and because a city full of tall buildings is the capital, it came to mean ‘capital city.’
Picture 日 (sun) shining over 京 (capital city): a sunlit capital makes a fine view, so 景 means ‘scenery.’ 京 also gives the sound jǐng.

历 means ‘to pass through, experience’ and also ‘calendar.’ Picture the raised paths on dykes between rice paddies, the main way people get around in parts of rural China. 厂 (slope) may stand for those paths, and 力 (lì) gives the sound.
盾 means ‘shield’: picture an eye 目 peeking out from behind a shield 厂. Pair it with 矛 (spear) and you get 矛盾 máodùn, ‘spear-shield,’ which means ‘contradiction.’
Picture 十 (ten) 目 (eyes) checking the line 一 underneath, and every one of them agrees it is straight. 直 also gives its sound to several other characters.
食 shows a jar people kept food in. The 人 on top is its lid, sitting over 良, the pot below. Lift the lid and it's time to eat.
Put 亻 (person) beside 两 ‘two’ and you have two people, a pair. 两 also supplies the sound, so liǎ sounds close to liǎng.
Picture a chariot seen from overhead: the top and bottom horizontal strokes of 车 are its two wheels, and the line running between them is the axle-and-body frame. That's a ‘vehicle.’
辆 puts 车 (vehicle) together with 两 (two), but it doesn't mean ‘two cars.’ It's the word you use to count vehicles, and 两 also gives it the sound liàng.
辶 (movement, walking) signals going somewhere, and 反 (fǎn) supplies the sound, so 返 fǎn means to go back or return.
木 (wood) tells you this is a wooden board or plank. 反 (fǎn) gives the sound, though today it's only a rough hint for bǎn.

唐 first meant boasting, or talking big, which is why it has 口 (mouth) in it. The dynasty name came later, when the character was borrowed for its sound. The ‘exaggerated’ sense still carries that loud-talk meaning.
米 (rice) marks grainy, powdery foods like sugar, and 唐 (táng) gives the sound. Think of sugar as sweet granules, like tiny grains of rice.
Put 讠 (words) next to 舌 (tongue) and you get what a tongue does with words: talk, speech, language.
A person 人 sits on top of a tongue 舌. Picture people sharing a deep, tongue-filled kiss where no one can see them, in their own home.

事 pictures a hand gripping a writing tool, like a scribe on duty. Scribes held office and served early rulers, so the character first meant ‘to serve’ and came to mean an affair or matter of business.
To sing, you open your mouth wide the way you do in a yawn, and that's what 欠 (yawn, open mouth) shows. 哥 (gē) gives the sound, so 歌 means ‘song’ or ‘to sing.’
夂 merges two old radicals, one for ‘follow’ and one for ‘slow.’ Its shape suggests a person taking a big step forward, so it's easy to tie to the idea of going.
Under the 宀 (roof), 各 (each) person who comes in is treated as a guest. 各 also hints at the sound kè.
乞 used to be the same as 气 ‘breath, vapor’. It was probably borrowed for its sound to mean ‘to beg’, so you can think of a beggar's breathy plea.
A 口 (mouth) sits beside 乞 (to beg), like a hungry mouth pleading for food, so the character means ‘to eat.’ 乞 also gives the sound.
尸 began as a drawing of a man lying flat, a body stretched out and not getting up, which is why it means ‘corpse.’ Don't mix it up with 户 (door), which has an extra stroke on top.

Picture a spring, 泉 (water source), bubbling out from under a cliff 厂. The first meaning was ‘spring’, and a spring is where water starts, so 原 means source or origin. The water at the bottom later turned into 小 (small).

Being willing comes from the 心 (heart), which sits under 原 (yuán), the part that gives the sound yuàn. The traditional form puts a ‘head’ radical where the modern one has 心, as if willingness moved from the head down to the heart.

音 started as 言 (speech) with an extra stroke inside the mouth, marking the voice that speech makes. Over time it changed shape into 立 ‘stand’ on top of 日, so picture a sound rising up out of an open mouth.
意 puts 音 (sound, tone) over 心 (heart). Think of an idea as the tone humming in your heart, the inner voice behind your thoughts and motives.
爫 is the form 爪 (claws) takes inside other characters. It always sits at the top, like a claw reaching down to grab whatever is below it.
Picture 冖 as an object being handed down from 爫 (a clawed hand) at the top to 又 (a right hand) at the bottom. The lower hand takes it, so 受 means ‘to receive.’
The older form of 爱 ‘love’ had 心 (heart) in its middle. In the simplified form the heart is gone and 友 (friend) sits at the bottom, so love means holding a friend close.

仁 joins 亻 (person) with 二 (two), and the two can stand for ‘another person’: humaneness is how you treat others. It's also probably related to 人 rén, ‘person’, and it's one of the core Confucian virtues.
乍 means ‘suddenly’ and rarely stands alone. When you spot it inside a larger character, it usually gives the sound zha.
A 乍 (sudden) burst of 火 (fire) is an explosion. 乍 also gives the sound zhà.
Picture 宀 (roof) sitting over 八 (eight): a rocky roof arching over an opening. That's the mouth of a cave, so 穴 means a cave, den or hole.
Picture yourself walking through a 穴 (cave) when the passage 乍 (suddenly) squeezes tight. That's narrow! 乍 also hints at the sound, zhǎi.
Think of 昌 as two suns stacked up, with the lower one written as 曰. Sun plus sun gives the meaning ‘sunlight, splendor.’
You sing with your 口 (mouth), and that's where the meaning comes from. 昌 (chāng) hints at the sound chàng.
Thinking takes both your head and your heart 心. The top began as a head, but over time it turned into 田 ‘field’. Picture your heart tending a field of thoughts.
Picture 乡 as a road twisting its way down a hillside into the countryside. Follow that winding path and you reach the village, far from the city.
巾 is a picture of a small cloth hanging down: 冂 is the drooping edges of a towel or napkin, and 丨 is the line it hangs from.
The top of 冒 is a cover sitting over 目 (eye), so it first meant covering the eyes. If you charge ahead with your eyes covered, you're taking a risk, which is how it came to mean to brave or to dare.
巾 (cloth) signals the meaning and 冒 gives the sound mào. Picture a piece of cloth pulled down over your eye (目 inside 冒) and you've got a hat.
The sun 日 marks the passing of days, and a single stroke 丨 stands beside it. Picture something that has watched many suns go by: it's old. This means old for things, not people.
戴 means to wear things like hats or glasses, and also to honor. To remember its parts, think of 十 (ten) 戈 (lances) farming a 田 (field) 共 (together).

水 is a drawing of flowing water: the long central stroke is the main current, and the strokes on each side are splashes along its banks. When it sits on the left side of other characters, it shrinks to 氵 (water).
酉 is a picture of a wine jug, and the horizontal stroke inside it is the wine. Watch the difference from 西 (west): 酉 has that extra line of liquid.
Liquid 氵 (water) poured from 酉 (a wine jar) gives you wine or liquor. 酉 also helps with the sound, jiǔ.
Look at the pieces: a hand 又 reaches over and seizes an ear 耳. Grabbing someone by the ear is how you remember 取, ‘to take’ or ‘to grab.’
躺 means to lie down. 身 (body) on the left hints at the meaning, and 尚 on the right once supplied the sound.
趟 is how you count trips. 走 (walk) gives the meaning, since you walk to get somewhere, and 尚 gives the sound.
常 first meant long trailing threads, which is why 巾 (cloth) sits at the bottom. 尚 on top gives the sound cháng. Today the character means ‘often’ or ‘common.’
手 (hand) at the bottom tells you this is about the palm. 尚 (shàng) on top gives the sound zhǎng. Holding something in your palm is also how you come to be in charge of it.
A reward usually means money, so 贝 (cowrie shell, ‘money’) sits at the bottom of 赏. The 尚 on top gives the sound shǎng.
革 is a drawing of an animal hide that's been cut open and laid out flat to dry. Picture a cowhide stretched out in the sun, and you have ‘leather.’
The left part, now written 又 (right hand), began as a drawing of a man whose hands are bound behind him. Someone tied up like that is in real trouble, so 艰 means difficult or hardship.

谷 is a picture of a valley: the top strokes 八 and 人 are like slopes opening out, and 口 is the valley's mouth down below. Its ‘grain’ meaning is a modern add-on, because 谷 now serves as the simplified form of a different, unrelated character.
Picture a 宀 (roof) sheltering a pile of 谷 (grain). The house lets the harvest in and holds it, which is how 容 comes to mean ‘to contain’ or ‘to allow.’
勿 started as a knife 勹 with strokes 丿 marking the scraps it cuts away. Scraps are things you don't need, and that idea grew into ‘don't!’ or ‘must not.’
易 began as a drawing of a chameleon, the lizard that changes its colors, which is how it came to mean ‘to change.’ The sense ‘easy’ was probably borrowed later because the words sounded alike.
聪 starts with 耳 (ear) because it first meant quick of hearing. Someone who catches things fast by ear also understands fast, so the meaning grew into ‘clever.’ 总 on the right gives the sound cōng.
Put 日 (sun) next to 月 (moon) and you have the two brightest lights in the sky side by side, so 明 means ‘bright’ or ‘clear’.

听 means ‘to listen.’ Its older, fuller form had an ear among its meaning parts, and today's form is a shortened version of it. To remember it, imagine words from 口 (mouth) travelling across to reach an ear, played here by 斤.
今 (now, the present) sits on top of 心 (heart, mind). When you hold what's in front of you right now in your mind, you're thinking about it or studying it.
耂 (old person) sits right on top of 子 (child). Picture a child holding up an elderly parent, and you have filial piety: caring for your elders.

On the left, an elder (the top of 考 ‘old’) stands over 子 ‘child’, and 攵 is a hand holding a stick for discipline: that is teaching. Originally the top part was a crisscross mark, the stroke the child was learning to write.
The top of 曷 is 曰 ‘say’, not 日 ‘sun’. Picture someone speaking up to ask ‘what?’ or ‘why?’ This question word shows up mostly in formal, literary writing.
豕 is a drawing of a pig. Tip your head to one side and you can see its body, its legs and its tail hanging down.
A pig 豕 sheltered under a roof 宀 makes a home. Back then a pig was something a family valued a lot, so the place where it was kept stood for the household itself.
户 is a drawing of a door, and it also counts households, one door per family. Watch the little dot 丶 on top: without it you get 尸 ‘corpse’.

方 may have started as a drawing of a man leaning far over to one side, so think ‘side’ and ‘direction’. It was once how 旁 (side) was written, and today 方 means ‘square’ and also gives the fang sound to other characters.
A house or room starts with a door: 户 (door) gives the meaning, and 方 (fāng) supplies the sound fáng.
To visit someone or dig up news, you have to talk, so 讠 (speech) gives the meaning. 方 (fāng) gives the sound fǎng.
纟 (silk thread) tells you this is about thread, so 纺 means to spin fibers into yarn. 方 (fāng) on the right gives the sound fǎng.
To imitate is to copy a person, and 亻 (person) gives that meaning. 方 (fāng) gives the sound fǎng.
阝 (mound) brings to mind earthen ramparts that guard against attack, and 方 (fāng) gives the sound fáng.
妨 (to hinder) puts 女 ‘woman’ beside 方 (fāng), which gives the sound fáng. The woman part carrying the meaning ‘hinder’ shows a sexist bias from the all-male scribes who shaped the script.
攵 (a hand doing an action) points to the meaning: the hand lets something go or puts it down. 方 (fāng) gives the sound fàng.
至 began as a picture of an arrow coming down and hitting the ground 土 (earth). The arrow has reached its target, so the character means ‘reach, arrive.’
Here 尸 stands for lying or sitting down, and 至 means ‘to arrive.’ A room is the place you reach when you want to lie down or take a seat.
戊 started out as a drawing of a halberd, a spear with an axe-like blade partway up the shaft. It looks a lot like 戈 (lance). Today it's used as the fifth heavenly stem.
A city starts with its walls, built from 土 (earth). 成 (chéng) gives the sound, so 城 is chéng, a ‘city wall’ and then the city itself.

交 shows a man standing with his legs crossed, so it first meant ‘to cross.’ Things that cross paths meet and pass between each other, which is where ‘to hand over’ and ‘to exchange’ come from. 交 also gives the sound jiāo to several other common characters.
Picture students at school passing 木 (trees) to each other, since 交 means ‘hand over.’ 交 also hints at the sound xiào.
The 阝 on the right stands for ‘city’ and gives the meaning: land around a city, its suburbs or outskirts. 交 (jiāo) gives the sound.
犭 (dog) stands for a small animal here, and small animals get a reputation for being sly. Think of calling a sneaky person ‘foxy.’ 交 gives the sound jiǎo.
胶 means glue or anything sticky. The ⺼ (meat) on the left probably points to the meaning, and 交 (jiāo) gives the sound. Think of tendons that join 交 the muscles ⺼ together.
Think of the lower part 㠯 as a pair of buttocks under 宀 (roof): an official who just sits around in his office and gets nothing done.
Picture an official 官 sitting down to eat 饣 (food) at a public hall or eatery. 官 (guān) also gives the sound, guǎn.
Today 尼 looks like 尸 (corpse) over 匕 (ladle), but it began as two people side by side, possibly meaning ‘be near.’ The meaning ‘nun’ was borrowed only for its sound.

尼 (ní) gives the sound, and 口 ‘mouth’ tells you it's a spoken particle. 呢 can mark a question, a thoughtful pause, or a gentle warning. The meaning ‘wool’ is a sound-loan, borrowed only for its pronunciation.
Put 户 (door) together with 斤 (axe) and you get building a home to live in. That's why 所 means ‘place,’ a spot where someone has settled.
Add 氵 (water) to 气 (breath, vapor) and you get steam: water turned into a breath-like cloud. 气 also gives the sound qì.
舟 (boat) on the left gives 船 its meaning. In modern Chinese, 舟 by itself mostly means a small boat, while 船 covers any vessel, from a little rowboat to a big ship.
飞 is a stripped-down drawing of a bird in flight. The hooked stroke is its body sweeping up, and the little strokes are its flapping wings, so the character means ‘to fly.’
几 is a drawing of a small table on two legs. Its meanings ‘how many’ and ‘a few’ come from borrowing its sound, not from the picture.
行 is made of two ‘step’ pieces side by side: 彳 on the left and a slightly changed step, 亍, on the right. Step after step means you're on the move, so 行 means ‘to go’ or ‘to walk’.
圭 stacks two 土 (earth) signs. These jade tablets were symbols of authority, handed over when a ruler granted someone land, so ‘earth’ appears twice.
A street is somewhere you walk, so 行 (walk, go) wraps around the character and gives the meaning. 圭 (guī) sits in the middle and once gave the sound.
Put things right under your 宀 (roof) and life feels settled and fixed. The bottom part started out as 正 ‘set right’ but now looks like 疋.
Something happens 乍 (suddenly) to your 心 (heart/mind), and you're left puzzled, asking ‘how? why?’
Two 人 (person) walk in single file, one behind the other. So 从 means ‘to follow,’ and from there ‘from’ or ‘since.’
回 shows a small 口 inside a bigger 囗, like a swirl or whirlpool that circles round and round until it gets back to where it started. That's why it means ‘to return.’
至 (reach) gives the meaning of arriving somewhere. 刂 (knife, dāo) supplies the sound dào. When you reach the place, you've arrived.
Two 人 (people) sit facing each other on 土 (earth). They've plopped down on the ground, so 坐 means ‘to sit.’ It also means to ride in a vehicle, since you sit to travel.
Under the shelter of 广 (roof), 坐 (sit), which shows two 人 people on 土 earth, gives you a seat indoors. 坐 also gives the sound zuò.

来 started out as a drawing of a wheat plant growing in the field, and ‘wheat’ was its original meaning. Because the word for ‘wheat’ sounded like the word for ‘to come,’ the character was borrowed to write ‘come.’
去 began as a drawing of a lidded cup. The lid turned into 土 (earth) on top, and the cup turned into 厶 at the bottom. Nobody knows how it came to mean ‘to go.’
To get walking, 走 (walk), you first have to rise and start moving. 己 (jǐ) gives 起 its sound, qǐ.
日 (sun, day) points to the meaning ‘yesterday’, the day that just went by. 乍 (zhà) on the right once supplied the sound.
Picture 日 (sun) sitting just over the line 一 (horizon): the sun has only just come up, so 旦 means dawn. It also lends its sound dàn to a few other characters.
扌 (hand) shows the work of carrying a load on a shoulder pole, and 旦 (dàn, ‘dawn’) gives the sound dān. Hands and shoulders share the burden.
⺼ (flesh) tells you 胆 is a body organ, the gallbladder, which also stands for courage. 旦 (dàn) gives the sound dǎn.
免 started as a drawing of a woman giving birth, with her legs spread. That sense now belongs to 娩, which adds 女 (woman) to make it clear. 免 itself came to mean ‘to spare’ or ‘to escape.’
晚 pairs 日 (sun) for the meaning with 免 (miǎn), which once gave the sound. Think of the time of day when the sun is going away: evening, late.
工 is a picture of a carpenter's square, the tool a builder uses to get corners right. Picture a craftsman holding it and you have ‘work.’

经 first meant the warp: the lengthwise threads stretched on a loom, which the right side pictures. 纟 (silk thread) makes the idea clearer. Threads that run all the way through lead to ‘pass through’ and ‘experience,’ and to the classics.
还 puts 辶 (movement) together with 不. Here 不 does not mean ‘not’. It's a simplified stand-in for the top-right part of the traditional form 還, so don't read it as negation.
剪 means ‘scissors’ or ‘to cut.’ 前 (front) on top gives the sound jiǎn, and 刀 (knife) underneath points to cutting.
Fire dots 灬 under the pan mean cooking over heat: frying or simmering. The 前 (qián, ‘front’) on top gives the sound jiān.
日 (sun) moving across the sky next to 寸 (inch, a unit of measure) gives you the idea of measuring the sun's progress, and that is time.
白 (bái, ‘white’) on the bottom gives 百 its sound, bǎi. The 一 ‘one’ on top tells you it's a number: one hundred.
Find 力 (strength) with two little dots 丶 around it. Put a couple of points of strength to work and you're doing something, so 为 means ‘to do’ or ‘to act.’
Picture 弟 (little brother) wearing a hat of ⺮ (bamboo). He stands in line with his siblings, waiting to be called first, second, third. 第 marks those ordinals, and 弟 gives it the sound dì.

年 started out as 禾 (grain) sitting over 亻 (person): someone hauling in the crop. The grain harvest comes once each cycle, so the character came to mean ‘year.’ The modern shape no longer shows those two pieces clearly.
凵 is a picture of an open bowl, with sides curving up and an empty top ready to hold things. That's why it means a container.
屮 is a picture of a sprout: the stem 丨 shoots straight up, and the cup shape 凵 forms the two little leaves opening on either side.
Picture a little sprout 屮 pushing up and out of a bowl 凵. That's 出: to come or go out, and also to produce.
Besides ‘to wait’ and ‘rank,’ 等 often closes a list, like ‘etc.’ In 马、牛、羊等 it can simply mean ‘horses, cows, and sheep.’ Doubled, 等等 means ‘and so on.’
Picture a heart 忄 that takes its time, lazily watching the sun 日, a hat 罒 and a hand 又 go by. That's 慢, ‘slow.’ The right side 曼 (màn) also gives the sound.
井 is a picture of a well. You can also read the grid as eight family fields around a shared middle plot, and the village well sits in that center square.
礻 (spirit, altar) often marks characters about religion. Here it points to rituals honoring the spirits, which grew into manners and courtesy. 乚 gives the sound lǐ.
拜 means to worship or pay respects. Its earliest form put 手 (hand) together with a plant, meaning worship with the harvest. Today you can think of it as two 手 hands side by side, joined in respect.
合 means ‘to join’ and 手 is ‘hand’. Bring the fingers of your hand together and you pick something up and hold it.
A man 大 (big) sits locked inside 囗 (enclosure), which makes it a prison. There's always a cause for someone being jailed, so 因 means ‘cause’ or ‘because’.
A person 亻 standing beside his 言 (words) keeps his promise. That makes him sincere, someone you can trust and believe.
The older full form of 万 began as a drawing of a scorpion. The meaning ‘ten thousand’ was borrowed only because the words sounded alike, so you can picture a swarm of ten thousand scorpions.
正 means ‘straight, correct’: a foot 止 stops right at the line 一. It has exactly five strokes, so people tally things in groups of five by writing 正 one stroke at a time.
正 (upright, correct) gives the sound zhèng, and 攵 means ‘strike’ or ‘knock’. Picture a government keeping order by force: the power to rule comes backed by a stick.

The top, 敕 ‘to correct; imperial orders’, is built from 束 (bundle, bind) plus 攵 (knock). Tie things up, knock them into shape, and you get something neat and orderly. 正 at the bottom gives the sound zhěng.
彳 (step) points to setting out on a journey or expedition, and 正 (zhèng) gives the sound zhēng.
疒 shows a person lying stretched out on a bed. Someone who stays in bed like that is sick, so this part marks characters about illness.
A stroke 丿 slashes right through 心 (heart). Picture that sharp cut and think: this has to happen, it's a must.

心 ‘heart-mind’ gives the meaning and 亡 (wáng) gives the sound: something slips out of your mind and you forget it. Don't mix it up with 忙 ‘busy’, which uses the same parts but puts 忄 (the side form of heart) on the left.
刻 first meant ‘to carve’: 刂 (knife) gives the cutting sense, and 亥 (hài) hints at the sound. Its ‘quarter of an hour’ meaning comes from a transliteration.
Picture a person 人 stepping into an enclosed space marked by the borders 冂. Once they're past those walls, they're inside.
Picture yourself walking along 辶 ‘walk’ and stepping just one 寸 ‘inch’ farther, and you've gone over to the other side. That's 过: to pass or go across.
自 is a drawing of a nose, and the same shape sits on top of 鼻 (nose). When people in China mean ‘me,’ they point at their nose, so 自 means ‘self.’
A clawing hand 爫 reaches down over a tree 木 to pluck its fruit, so 采 means to pick or gather.
Think of 具 as a Cyclops wearing a ⺮ (bamboo) hat. Together, ⺮ (bamboo) and 具 also suggest a bamboo abacus, so 算 means to calculate or count.
讠 (speech) gives the meaning and 人 (person, rén) gives the sound rèn. 人 stands in for an older, more complicated sound part. Think of words 讠 that help you recognize a person 人.
A road is where your feet go: 足 (foot) on the left gives the meaning, and 各 on the right once gave the sound.
疒 (sickness) marks the meaning, and 丙 (bǐng) gives the sound, which is close to bìng. Put together, they mean ‘illness’.
Picture a rich, bountiful 丰 land dotted with 阝 (city) settlements. Put them together and you have a whole nation.
邦 (bāng) on top gives the sound. The 巾 ‘cloth’ below is a shortened form of an older ‘riches’ part, which may hint that working together and helping each other is how wealth gets built.
To tie something up, you use cord, so 纟 (silk thread) gives the meaning. 邦 (bāng) gives the sound bǎng.
垂 started as a drawing of a tree with its leaves drooping down. Picture those limp, hanging leaves and you have its meaning: to hang or dangle.
When your 目 (eye) starts to 垂 (droop), you're nodding off to sleep. 垂 (chuí) also hints at the sound shuì.
犬 began as a drawing of a dog. Over time the drawing got simplified into 大 ‘big’ plus a dot 丶, so picture a big dog with one floppy ear. Watch the dot's position so you don't mix it up with 太.
A 犬 (dog) sits under two 口 (mouths), howling, and that howl gives 哭 its meaning ‘to cry, to wail.’ The same top also appears in the traditional form 喪 ‘to mourn.’
平 is drawn as a set of scales hanging perfectly balanced. When both sides sit even, everything is level and calm, which gives the meanings ‘flat, level, peaceful.’
评 puts 讠 (words) together with 平 (to weigh). Weighing something up in words is how you judge or criticize it. 平 also gives 评 its sound, píng.
Put 艹 (grass, standing for plants) on top of 平 (píng) and you get 苹 píng. 艹 marks it as something that grows, and 平 gives the sound. You'll meet it most in 苹果 ‘apple’.
怕 pairs 忄 (heart) with 白 ‘white,’ which mostly supplies the sound (bái → pà). To remember it, think of a heart gone white with fright, a bit like the English word ‘lily-livered’ for a coward.
办 is built on 力 (strength), because getting things done takes effort. Picture the two dots beside it as drops of sweat from someone hard at work handling a job.
错 first meant ‘to inlay’ metal decorations, which is why it has 钅 (metal/gold) on the left. That meaning is rare now, and today 错 mostly means a mistake, or wrong.

坏 means ‘bad’ or ‘spoiled.’ It has 土 (earth) on the left, and on the right something that looks like 不 ‘not.’ That 不 isn't really the negating word here. It's just a simplified stand-in for the more complex right side of the traditional form.
氵 (water) tells you this is about flowing water, a river. 可 (kě) gives the sound, which turns into hé.
永 is a picture of water currents, and 水 (water) sits right inside it. Think of a river that keeps flowing on and on, never stopping. That's why 永 means ‘forever, eternal.’
冫 (ice) is like 氵 (water) with one dot missing. Water has three drops, and once it freezes into ice only two are left.
Picture a line of people waiting for 冫 (ice), and the supply keeps running out: 欠 ‘lacking’. Each time, the next person in order is the one who goes without.
Picture a tiny 矢 (arrow) beside a little 豆 (bean): both are small, stubby things, so together they mean ‘short.’ 豆 also gives the sound.
比 is two 匕 ‘spoon’ shapes placed next to each other. The oldest forms showed two people standing side by side. Either way, you get two look-alike things lined up so you can compare them.
口 (mouth) shows you breathe in or suck in through your mouth. 及 (jí) once gave the sound, though it doesn't match xī closely anymore.
南 means ‘south.’ In compass directions, Chinese puts it last, so ‘southwest’ becomes 西南, literally ‘west-south.’
北 shows two people seated back to back, and it first meant ‘back’ (now written 背). ‘North’ came later, mostly because it sounded the same, with a small link in meaning too.
辶 (walk) points to walking along a border or edge. The piece inside looks like 力 ‘strength’, but it's really just a simplified stand-in for the sound part 臱.
牙 began as a drawing of a tooth, which is why it means ‘tooth’ or ‘fang.’ It also gives the sound yá to many common characters that contain it.
呀 is a sound that comes out of the 口 (mouth) when you're surprised: ‘ya!’ The 牙 (yá, ‘tooth’) part gives it its sound. It can also imitate noises, like a door creaking.
讠 (speech) plus 牙 yá ‘tooth’: you gasp out loud in surprise. 牙 also gives the sound, yà.
艹 (grass) on top tells you it's a plant, and 牙 (tooth, yá) below gives the sound. Picture a sprout poking up out of the soil like a little new tooth.

面 began as a drawing of a mask worn over a face, so it means ‘face’ or ‘surface.’ Because it sounds like the word for flour and noodles, it's also borrowed to write that word. The traditional form adds 麥 ‘wheat’ to show that meaning.
穿 puts 穴 (cave, hole) over 牙 (tooth). Picture a tooth biting a hole into something: making a hole is piercing, the main meaning. 穿 also means ‘to wear’.
辶 (walk) carries the meaning: you move along until you're near. 斤 (jīn) gives the sound jìn.
凵 was once a pit, and 乂 is a person tumbling into it with legs flailing upward. Falling into a pit is a disaster, so 凶 means bad luck, cruelty and calamity.
离 looks like a standing animal with 亠 as its head. Its main meaning today, ‘to leave’ or ‘from’, is borrowed: the character was taken over for its sound, not its picture.
Your face is made of flesh, so 脸 has ⺼ (meat/flesh) on the left for the meaning. The 佥 on the right used to give the character its sound.
Think of 母 (mother) with a cap on top: each mom wears a cap, so 每 means ‘each, every.’ 母 also gives the sound.
忄 (heart) sits next to 圣 ‘saint.’ Picture having a saint's heart: to everyone else, that seems strange and unusual.

Picture 月 (meat) and 犬 (dog) roasting over 灬 (fire). 然 originally meant ‘to roast,’ but it was borrowed for its sound to mean ‘so; naturally.’ The roasting sense moved to 燃, which adds one more 火 (fire).
午 started out as a drawing of a pestle and once meant ‘to knock against.’ It came to mean ‘noon’ only because it was borrowed for its sound. Picture a pestle pounding at midday.
Picture a round fruit, drawn as 田, hanging on top of a tree 木. Fruit is what a tree yields in the end, so 果 means ‘fruit’ and also ‘result’.
Look for three 十 (ten) joined together in 世, with the left upright bent to fit the design. Three tens make thirty years, about the length of one generation.
Put 氵 (water) beside 每 ‘every’: gather every drop of water and you get the sea. 每 (měi) also hints at the sound hǎi.
A 口 (mouth) sits on top of 八 (eight). Picture a quiet person whose mouth lets out only eight words, just a few and nothing more. That gives you 只, ‘only, merely.’
Imagine an ox 牛 ‘ox’ living inside a temple 寺 ‘temple’. That's no ordinary cow, it's special! 寺 also gives the sound (tè).
氵 (water) tells you the meaning is ocean. 羊 ‘sheep’ (yáng) gives the sound, so 洋 is also read yáng.
江 means a large river, and the Yangtze in particular. 氵 (water) gives the meaning. 工 was once the sound part, though today it doesn't sound much like jiāng.
Jade 玉 is put away 入 (enter) for safekeeping, so 全 means whole, entire, and also to preserve. Or think of the top as 人 (man) and the bottom as 王 (king): every man a king, which means all of them.
Picture two hands in a tug-of-war. ⺈ is a shortened hand on top and 彐 is a hand below, and both grab at the stick 亅. That's the idea of fighting over something or arguing about it.
Picture people fighting over 冫 (ice), since clean, pure ice is worth the struggle. 争 ‘to fight’ also gives 净 its sound, jìng.
业 shows a treetop full of dense leaves, a picture of busy growth and prosperity. That makes it a fitting sign for ‘business’ and ‘profession’: work that flourishes.
Picture 兄 ‘elder brother’ putting on a fancy hat, the top of 尚, before he heads off to a party meeting. 尚 also gives the sound dǎng.
Think of 车 (chariot) rolling into battle loaded with 斤 (axes), ready to chop and behead. That's 斩, ‘to cut’ or ‘to sever’.
Picture 斩 (chop) slicing across 日 (sun) so the light is cut off, but only for a short while. That's 暂, ‘temporary.’ 斩 also hints at the sound zàn.
The traditional form 發 contains 弓 (bow), a hint at shooting or sending something out, and its 殳 (club) part was once an arrow. The simplified 发 also means ‘hair’ only because it sounds the same.
Imagine someone standing by a 井 (well) and giving a talk, with 讠 (speech) beside it. 讠 tells you the meaning is about speaking or explaining, and 井 (jǐng) hints at the sound jiǎng.
Imagine passing a message along through one special person: 亻 (person) is the carrier, and 专 (special, sole) gives the sound chuán. Together they mean ‘to pass on’ or ‘to transmit.’
Picture turning your one and only 车 (cart) around. 专 (sole, only) gives the sound zhuǎn, and the wheels of 车 carry the idea of turning and moving.
A brick is one single block of 石 ‘stone’, and 专 means ‘sole, special’. 专 also gives the sound zhuān.
虫 began as a drawing of a bug, so picture it as a little creature with a body and legs. The traditional form, 蟲, stacks three of them, like a whole swarm of bugs.
Picture a tiny 虫 (insect) with a big 口 (mouth) on top: although it has a mouth, it's still just a little bug. That ‘although’ is what 虽 means.
象 began as a picture of an elephant. It also works as a short form of 像 (to look like), which gives it the meanings image, likeness and portrait.
像 began as the same word as 象 ‘elephant; image’. 亻 (person) was added later to make the meaning of a likeness or image clearer, and 象 still gives the sound xiàng.
Look at the top of 亮 and you'll see 高 (tall) with its bottom 口 (mouth) missing. Under it sits 几 (table). Picture a tall table that's bright because it's been cleared of its mouth.
瓦 (pottery) marks a vessel of fired clay, since bottles and vases were first made of clay. 并 (bìng) hints at the sound píng.
扌 (hand) shows you use your hands to put pieces together, and 并 (bìng, ‘combine’) gives the sound pīn.
To stay alive, you need 氵 (water) on your 舌 (tongue). A dry tongue can't live long.
Picture a boulder that has tumbled down and come to rest under a cliff 厂. The 口 here isn't a ‘mouth’. It's that rock lying at the bottom, so 石 means stone.
亦 started out as a picture of a man with a mark on each side showing his armpits, so it first meant ‘armpit.’ It was later borrowed for its sound to mean ‘also,’ and armpit is now written 腋.
变 is 亦 (also) on top of 又 (right hand). To remember it, picture the right hand making a change as well.
步 began as a drawing of two feet, one ahead of the other. The top 止 is a foot, so picture yourself taking step after step as you walk.
Here 尸 shows a person lying down to sleep, and the place where you sleep is where you live. 古 (old) once gave the sound.
Picture getting slashed by a 刂 (knife) inside your own 居 (residence). That's a severe, dramatic scene, fit for a stage play. 居 (jū) also hints at the sound jù.
One 火 (fire) is stacked on another 火 (fire). With twice the fire, it blazes and gets very hot.
讠 (speech) tells you it's about words, and 炎 (yán, ‘blaze’) gives the sound, read tán here. Picture a conversation so lively it blazes: that's 谈, to talk or chat.
Think of 击 as 二 (two strokes) smashing down into 山 (mountain) so the two overlap. That collision is a strike or hit.
Picture a hand 扌 closing tightly around a little pill 丸. That firm grip is the core idea of 执: to grasp and hold, and from there to take charge or carry something out.
斗 began as a drawing of an old scoop for measuring grain by the peck. Its sound was later borrowed for dòu ‘to fight’, and that loaned meaning is now the main one.
Picture a market 市 set up at the city gate 门 (gate). It's noisy and crowded, and fights keep breaking out, so 闹 means lively or rowdy, and also to make a disturbance or quarrel.

Think of 丶 (a dot) as some object tossed under 几 (a small table). It's just any ordinary thing you'd leave down there, which gives you ‘common’ and ‘any’. This is only a memory trick, not where the character really comes from.
Fear is something you feel in the 心 (heart), which sits at the bottom. The top part, 巩 (gǒng), hints at the sound kǒng.
虍 began as a drawing of a tiger. Put legs under it and you get the full character 虎 (tiger).
The crossed strokes 乂 on top show a cloth woven so loosely that its threads are rare, sitting above 布 (cloth). The common meaning ‘hope’ is only borrowed for its sound.
红 first meant a pinkish-red kind of thread, so it has 纟 (silk) on the left. 工 on the right gives the sound hóng.
切 means ‘to cut’ or ‘to slice,’ and the 刀 (knife) on the right shows the meaning. The 七 on the left gives the sound.
A bag or pocket is made of cloth, so 衣 (clothing) at the bottom gives the meaning. 代 on top gives the sound dài.
When there's 禾 (grain) for every 口 (mouth), people live in peace and harmony. 禾 also gives the sound hé.
Imagine a person 亻 stirring a potion with a ladle 匕, like an alchemist turning one substance into another. That's 化: to change or transform.
Picture 米 (rice) sitting on top of 大 (big): one kind of rice with really big grains. Sorting rice by kind helps you remember 类 means ‘kind, category.’
Picture a person 亻 sitting down in the shade of a tree 木 for a break. That's 休, ‘to rest.’
息 puts 自 (nose) on top of 心 (heart). Air moves through your nose while your heart keeps beating, so the character means breath, and from there rest or a pause.
Picture a craftsman who works with an awl 弋 and a measuring square 工. Measuring carefully makes every piece match a set pattern, so 式 means a form, model, or style.
癶 is two feet, each a form of 止 (foot/toe), pointing away from each other. Feet set back to back give it the sense ‘back-to-back’ or ‘opposed.’ You'll see it only as a part inside other characters.

豆 is a drawing of an old food vessel: a lid 一 on top, the bowl 口 in the middle, and a stand underneath. It came to mean ‘bean, pea’ only because the words sounded alike, so the shape has nothing to do with beans.
A lamp holds a flame, so 灯 has 火 (fire) on the left for the meaning. 丁 (dīng) on the right gives the sound dēng.
Picture things lined up 並 (side by side) under 日 (sun). Everywhere the sun shines, its light reaches all of them, so 普 means ‘universal, general.’

甬 may have started as a picture of a big bell, with the hook on top for hanging it. Some see a bucket in it instead. Today it's the name of the Yong River and short for Ningbo, the city on that river.
Picture 雨 (rain) pounding down on 田 (a field) while thunder booms overhead. That storm scene gives you 雷, ‘thunder.’

申 started out as a drawing of a lightning bolt. Think of a flash that stretches straight down through a field: the vertical 丨 cuts through the middle. That stretching bolt helps you remember ‘to extend’ and ‘to declare.’
