The hooked stroke 乚 is a bolt of lightning streaking down. The traditional form 電 adds 雨 (rain) on top, so it's a storm flash, and that's where ‘electricity’ comes from.
A person 亻 next to 申 (shēn) means to stretch or extend. 申 gives the sound shēn and also adds to the sense of reaching out.
女 (woman) tells you it's a female relative, and 审 gives the sound shěn. Don't just think ‘aunt’: Chinese kinship terms are exact, and 婶 means only your father's younger brother's wife.
Picture someone under a 宀 (roof), maybe a courtroom, laying out a statement with care while it gets examined closely. 申 gives the sound shěn.
Look for 日 (sun) at the bottom of 春. The strokes above it stand for plants shooting up under that sun, and a sunny sprouting time is spring.
兆 is a picture of the cracks that form on a tortoise shell when it's heated. In ancient China people read these cracks to tell the future, so the character means ‘omen.’
跳 means ‘to leap.’ The left side, 足 (foot), shows it's something you do with your feet, and 兆 (zhào) on the right hints at the sound tiào.
辶 (walking, moving) tells you someone is on the move: they're running away. 兆 (zhào) provides the sound. It rhymes with táo but doesn't match it exactly.
杀 means ‘to kill.’ The traditional form 殺 also had 殳 (a club) as its meaning part. Simplification removed the club, so 杀 is just the old sound element that remained.

Picture a 亻 (person) living off in a remote 谷 (valley) in the mountains, a backwoods type with country habits. That gives you ‘common, unrefined,’ and also ‘folk customs.’ It's only a memory trick, not the real origin.
A person next to a pile of bones means death. 歹 is ‘bone fragments’, and 匕 (ladle) started out as a drawing of a person that changed shape over time.
Picture 禾 (grain) beside 火 (fire). Once the harvest is threshed, farmers pile up the leftover stalks and burn them, and those smoky field fires are a typical sight in autumn.
冫 (ice) on the left gives the ‘cool, cold’ meaning, and 京 supplies the sound liáng. The traditional form 涼 uses 氵 (water) in place of the ice.
A round 口 (mouth) sitting on a round 贝 (cowrie shell) first meant ‘round.’ Later the character was borrowed for its sound to mean ‘member’ or ‘staff.’

员 (yuán) once meant ‘round’ by itself. Putting 囗 (enclosure) around it makes the meaning clear: a ring that closes all the way around, so the character means ‘round’ or ‘circle’. 员 still gives the sound.
A hand holding a stick, 攵 (strike), taps at 己 ‘self’: give yourself a push and you change and improve.
To summon someone, you use your 口 (mouth) to call them over. The 刀 (knife, dāo) on top gives the sound. Picture waving a knife as you shout for someone to come.
绍 first meant tying threads together, which is why it has 纟 (silk thread). 召 (to summon) gives the sound shào. Joining threads leads to connecting people, as when you introduce someone.
管 first meant a pipe made of bamboo, so ⺮ (bamboo) sits on top. 官 ‘official’ gives the sound, and it may also account for the sense ‘to manage’, since officials are the ones in charge.
To exhort someone, you put 力 (strength) into your words. The 又 (right hand) carries no meaning here. It's just a simple stand-in for the old, complicated sound part.
Picture a single 女 (woman) sheltered beneath 宀 (roof). With one woman under the roof, the household is calm, so 安 means peace and being at ease.
安 (ān, ‘peace’) on top gives the sound, and 木 ‘wood’ underneath stands for a wooden table. Picture legal case files spread out on a wooden bench.
The top of 亭 is a shortened 高 ‘tall’, and 丁 at the bottom gives the sound tíng. Picture a tall little pavilion or kiosk rising over a nail-shaped post 丁.
Picture a 亻 (person) halting at a 亭 (pavilion) to rest: that's ‘to stop.’ 亭 gives the sound tíng and may also hint at the meaning.

The lower part of 量 started out as 重 (heavy) and later got worn down into 里 ‘village’. The 日 on top was first just a thing sitting on the scale, so the character shows something heavy being weighed and measured.
贝 (cowrie shell) stands for money and value, and 戋 (jiān) gives the sound. Put together, 贱 is something of little value: cheap and low.
Picture a person 㔾 on top of a cliff 厃, looking down at something that has fallen off. 危 means ‘dangerous, precarious’ and also ‘high,’ and 厃 gives the sound wēi.
On the left is a bowl of food, and on the right 旡 is a person turning their head away from it. They've finished eating, so the meal is done ‘already’.
辰 may picture an ancient stone tool for breaking up soil. Picture farmers heading out early in the day, or early in the year, to turn the earth with it.
The sun 日 sits on top of 辰, which here means ‘early.’ An early sun is the morning. 辰 also gives the sound chén.
石 (stone) gives 研 its meaning: grinding something fine against stone. 开 on the right once hinted at the sound. Grinding down a problem that carefully is how you study and research it.
Picture someone squeezing into a 穴 (cave) to hunt something out. That digging around is where ‘to look into, investigate’ comes from. 九 (nine, jiǔ) gives the sound jiū.
Picture a 头 (head) safe under a 宀 (roof). Someone sheltered at home is solid and real, which is why 实 means ‘real, true.’
简 first meant a bamboo slip for writing on, which is why ⺮ (bamboo) sits on top. 间 gives the sound jiǎn. Space on a narrow slip is tight, so picture having to keep your words simple and short.
钅 (metal) tells you this is a metal, and 同 (tóng, ‘same’) supplies the sound: tóng, copper or bronze.
A hollow stalk of ⺮ (bamboo) makes a natural tube, and 同 (tóng) gives the sound tǒng.
Picture 先 ‘ahead’ riding on 辶 (walk): the one you choose in an election is the one who moves ahead. 先 also hints at the sound, xuǎn.
The top was once 氐 ‘go down’, sitting over 日 (sun). When the sun goes down you get dusk and darkness, and when a person ‘goes dark’ they faint.
女 (woman) points to the meaning, marriage, and 昏 (hūn) gives the sound, so 婚 is also read hūn.
羽 is a drawing of two feathers standing side by side. Each 习 is one feather, and together they look like a pair of wings.
Put 力 (strength) next to 口 (mouth) and you have 加. Your words add to your muscle and boost a cause, so the character means ‘to add’ or ‘to increase’.
马 (horse) sits under 加 (jiā), which gives the sound jià. You harness a horse to pull a cart, and now you ‘drive’ cars, planes and boats too.
A frame or rack is usually built from 木 (wood), which sits at the bottom, and 加 (jiā, ‘add’) on top gives the sound jià. It's also the measure word for airplanes.
咖 is used only for its sound, to spell out borrowed foreign words like coffee (咖啡). 口 (mouth) marks it as a spoken sound, and 加 (jiā) hints at the pronunciation kā.
榜 began as a billboard, which is why it has 木 (tree, wood) on the left. 旁 (bàng) on the right gives the sound. Picture a wooden board where notices and lists of names get posted.
石 (stone) suggests something heavy, which fits 磅 as a pound, the unit you use when you weigh things. 旁 gives the sound.
A 女 (woman) beside a 口 (mouth): picture yourself copying exactly what a woman says, speaking just like her. That's 如, ‘like, as, as if.’
决 first meant water bursting through a bank. The traditional form 決 has 氵 (water), which is simplified here to 冫. Senses like ‘to burst’ and ‘to decide’ grew out of that original meaning.
忄 (heart) plus 生 (birth, shēng) gives 性: whatever your heart carries from the moment you're born, meaning your nature or temperament. 生 also hints at the sound xìng.
A 亻 (person) stands beside 呆 ‘dull, foolish’: picture someone keeping watch over a clueless friend so no harm comes to them. That's 保, to protect. 呆 also hints at the sound.
见 (see) carries the meaning of looking at or viewing. 又 (right hand) is only a simple stand-in for the old, complicated sound part.
礻 (spirit, sign) beside 土 (earth) first meant an altar to the land's spirits. The villagers who gathered there to worship grew into the idea of a community, and later a society.
Two men 夫 stand side by side over 日. Picture one of them calling out ‘swap!’ as he steps in to take the other's place, so the character means to replace or substitute for.
Put 亻 (person) next to 本 (root): the body is a person's root, the base everything else grows from.

示 is a drawing of an altar: a flat top with offerings resting on a stand. What happens at an altar is linked to ‘sign’ and ‘show’, which is where those meanings come from. On the left side of a character it's written 礻.
宀 (roof) sits over 示 (altar, spirits). Picture the altar a family keeps under its own roof to honor its ancestors, which is where 宗's meanings of ancestry, clan, and lineage come from.
寸 ‘thumb’ stands for a hand passing something over to 亻 (person). That's the idea of 付: handing over, paying, or giving.
符 first meant a bamboo tally, which is why ⺮ (bamboo) sits on top. 付 (to hand over) below gives the sound fú. From a marked tally it came to mean a symbol, tag, or written charm.
Meat (肉) left sitting too long spoils. The top part 府 gives the sound fǔ, and 肉 ‘meat’ underneath points to the meaning: rotting.
彡 is a picture of three slanting strokes, 丿丿丿, like streaks or tufts of hair. You'll rarely see it standing alone, but it often turns up as a part inside other characters.
Picture 士 (a knight) with a load, the stroke 丿, slung over his shoulder as he marches along. He's the ninth in line of the heavenly stems.
Picture yourself explaining everything to a sheep, one careful detail after another. 讠 (speech) gives the meaning, and 羊 ‘sheep’ (yáng) gives the rhyme of xiáng.
细 started as 纟 (silk) plus ‘head’, which together meant ‘hair’, and hair gives the sense of fine and thin. Over time the ‘head’ part got distorted, and today it's written 田.
Picture food on its way to your 口 (mouth): 未 means ‘not yet’, so you haven't tasted it yet, but you can already imagine the flavor. 未 also gives the sound wèi.
Picture a 舌 ‘tongue’ caught on a 乚 ‘hook’ and flailing around. That's pure chaos, so 乱 means disorder or anarchy.
Take away 氵 (water) and what's left was once a drawing of a stream splitting into branches. Add the water back and 派 means ‘to branch off,’ which is how a group splits into factions and sects.
To help someone, you lend them your 力 (strength). 且 was once the sound part, but it no longer hints well at the modern reading zhù.
Picture a 女 (woman) at the side of her master's 又 (hand), always ready to serve. Together they mean a servant or slave.
努 puts 奴 ‘slave’ over 力 ‘strength’. Picture a slave putting all their strength into the work, so it means to strive or work hard, like ‘slaving away’ at something. 奴 also gives the sound nǔ.
怒 puts 奴 (slave) on top of 心 (heart). Picture the rage boiling in a slave's heart, or the angry feelings an owner holds toward a slave. 奴 also gives the sound, nù.
廴 shows a man striding out on a march, which is why it means ‘to walk, to go.’ Don't mix it up with 辶, a similar-looking walking component.
A hand 扌 stands guard at the door 户, which means ‘to protect’. 户 also gives the sound hù.
Picture 日 (sun) sinking into grass: 艹 on top, and the 大 underneath was once grass too. The character first meant ‘dusk.’ Now it's borrowed for its sound to mean ‘don't’ or ‘none.’
木 (tree, wood) hints that 模 may first have meant a wooden frame, a form you shape things by. That fits ‘pattern’ and ‘model.’ 莫 (mò) gives the sound.
摸 means to touch or feel with your hand, so it has 扌 (hand) on the left. 莫 (mò) on the right gives the sound mō.
Put 氵 (water) next to 莫 ‘none’ and you get a place with no water: a desert. 莫 (mò) also gives the character its sound.
A tomb is dug into 土 (earth), which sits at the bottom of 墓. The 莫 (mò) on top gives the sound mù.
A curtain is made of cloth, so 巾 (cloth) sits at the bottom of 幕, and 莫 on top gives the sound mù.
Picture a 宀 (roof) so wide that under it you can 见 (see) 艹 (grass) growing. That's one spacious hall, which is why 宽 means broad. Together, 艹 and 见 make 苋, and 苋 hints at the sound.
县 started out as a drawing of a head (首) turned upside down. Its meaning ‘county, district’ came later, either through association or by borrowing the sound.
扌 (hand) shows you lift with your hands, and 台 gives the sound tái. It often means carrying something together, with two or more people lifting it between them.
弗 first meant ‘rope’: the 弓 shape is a cord lashing two sticks (丿丨) together. Its meaning ‘not, unwilling’ was borrowed later only for the sound.
其 means ‘his, her, its, their.’ Keep an eye out for it inside other characters, because there it often works as the sound part and hints at a reading like qí.
Older forms of 韦 had a foot on top and another on the bottom, like two people walking off in opposite directions. Its meanings today are ‘tanned leather’ and a surname.
An enclosing wall 囗 (enclosure) runs all the way around, which gives the idea of surrounding something. Inside it, 韦 gives the sound wéi.
A great, imposing figure is a person, so 亻 (person) gives the meaning, and 韦 (wéi) hints at the sound wěi.
充 means ‘to fill up,’ and it can also mean ‘to pretend to be.’ For the second meaning, think of 允 ‘true’ putting on a hat 亠 as a disguise, so now it only pretends.
贝 (cowrie shell, once used as money) at the bottom points to goods and trade, and 化 (huà) on top once gave the sound huò.
A 口 (mouth) next to 咸 (salty): picture a mouth full of something way too salty, and you yell! 咸 (xián) also hints at the sound hǎn.
Picture sprinkling something 咸 ‘salty’ on 冫 (ice): the ice shrinks away, so it decreases. 咸 also hints at the sound.
照 is built from 日 (sun) and 召, which gives the sound zhào, with 灬 (fire) added underneath for extra emphasis. Sun plus fire means plenty of light to shine on things.
而 started out as a drawing of a beard hanging down from the chin. Its sound was later borrowed for the word ‘and; and yet; but,’ and that meaning is the one it keeps today.
邮 means mail or post. 由 (yóu) gives the sound, and 阝 marks a ‘place’, so think of the post office as the place where your mail goes.
A tree 木 boxed in by an enclosure 囗 can't spread out. It's trapped, so 困 means being hemmed in or in difficulty.
角 is a drawing of an animal's horn. See the pointed tip at the top (⺈) and the ridged body of the horn below it, so 角 means ‘horn’ and also ‘corner’ or ‘angle’.
Picture a 刀 (knife) freeing the 角 (horn) from a 牛 (ox). That's where the idea of cutting something loose comes from, and it grows into untying, unfastening, and explaining.
纟 (silk thread) tells you this is about weaving, and 只 (zhǐ) gives the sound zhī. Think of working silk threads into cloth.
杂 looks like 九 ‘nine’ on top of 一 ‘one’ and 小 ‘small’, like a jumble of odds and ends thrown together. That's why it means mixed or miscellaneous.
The two dots ⺀ at the bottom stand for ice. Picture someone walking 夂 over frozen ground, and you have winter.
冫 (ice) on the left tells you the meaning: something icy is cold. 令 (lìng) on the right hints at the sound lěng.
Look at 皿 ‘dish’ with a single stroke 丿 inside. That stroke is the blood sitting in the dish, so 血 means ‘blood’. In casual speech people also say it as xiě.

The top of 昷 looks like 日 ‘sun’, but it started as a drawing of a man shut in a box, a prisoner. Put over 皿 (dish), it shows someone bringing a prisoner food. That kind act gives the sense of warmhearted, and so warm. 氵 (water) adds the idea of warm water.
肉 began as a picture of a piece of dried meat. Picture the strokes inside the 冂 frame as the streaks in a strip of jerky, and you have ‘meat.’
A star is a small sun: 日 (sun) on top points to the meaning of a shining light in the sky, and 生 (shēng) underneath once hinted at the sound xīng.
When people discuss something, they use 讠 (speech) to talk about 义 ‘justice’, and 义 (yì) also gives the sound.
智 puts 知 (to know) on top of 日. Think of that bottom part as 曰 (to say): 知 plus 曰 add up to wisdom. 知 also gives the sound, zhì.
A knife 刂 cutting grain 禾 at harvest time: the blade has to be sharp, and the harvest brings in your profit.
考 first meant ‘old’ and looks a lot like 老 (old), since both have 耂 on top. The ‘test’ meaning came from borrowing its sound. You can still picture a wise elder, 耂, giving you an exam.
彡 (streaks) are strands of hair, and 镸 ‘long’ tells you how they grow: long, flowing hair.
丬 began as a drawing of a bed. Turn it on its side and you can see the frame standing up. Today the everyday word for ‘bed’ is written 床.
酉 (wine jar) at the bottom points to fermentation, since sauces and pastes are fermented like wine. 丬 at the top gives the sound jiàng.
扌 (hand) plus 合 (bring together) means gathering things into your hands, so 拾 is ‘to pick up.’ On cheques and in account books it also stands for ‘ten,’ because it's much harder to alter than 十.
舟 (boat) on the left means sailing and navigating, and 亢 on the right gives the sound háng.
寄 first meant ‘to dwell,’ which explains the 宀 (roof) on top. 奇 underneath gives the sound jì. Staying under someone else's roof means relying on them, and from there come ‘entrust’ and ‘send.’
Things carried along on 氵 (water) drift and float, and water also rinses and bleaches. 票 (piào) supplies the sound. You also see it as the first syllable of 漂亮 piàoliang, ‘good-looking’.
Picture 风 (wind) carrying a 票 (ticket) off so it floats and flutters through the air. 风 gives the meaning, and 票 (piào) hints at the sound piāo.
To call out, you use your 口 (mouth), so it points to the meaning. 奂 on the right gives the huàn sound.
辶 (walking) adds a sense of movement, as in going after something or following it. That's the older meaning, and today the character means ‘suitable, comfortable’. 舌 (tongue) is the sound part.
革 (leather, hide) on the left marks 鞋 as footwear, even though traditional Chinese shoes were rarely leather. 圭 on the right gives the sound.
Read 德 as 彳 (step, meaning action) plus a squashed form of 真 (true) over 心 (heart). Acting with a true heart is virtue.
Imagine a beard 而 dripping under 雨 (rain): the thirsty crops below need that rain to grow.
To warn someone, you use 言 (words) to make them feel 敬 (respect, caution). Careful speech on top of wariness gives you an alert, and 敬 also hints at the sound jǐng.

Under a 宀 (roof), people hold a 祭 (worship) ceremony and then watch closely to see if the gods are pleased. That careful watching is the root of ‘to examine, to investigate.’ 祭 also hints at the sound.
Picture someone so poor they sleep in a 穴 (cave) and get by only on 力 (strength) from hard physical work. That's being destitute.
雪 (snow) puts 雨 (rain) over 彐. Think of snow as rain that you can pick up and hold in your hand.
Soup and broth are mostly liquid, so 汤 has 氵 (water) on the left. The right side, 昜, gives the sound tāng.
Picture a pot of 汤 (soup) sitting on 火 (fire). It gets hot enough to scald you. 汤 tāng also gives the sound tàng, and 火 tells you the meaning has to do with heat.
耒 means ‘plow.’ Look for 木 (tree) inside it, then two extra strokes that stand for the plow's blades.
享 started as a picture of a covered dish for food offerings, with 亠 as the lid on top. Offering food and receiving it leads to the meaning ‘to enjoy’ or ‘to share’.
Picture four 口 (vessels) set around a 犬 (dog), like a dog watching over the dishes. The character may first have meant a sacrificial rite that used dogs. Today it means vessel, tool, or instrument.

Picture 大 (a big man) sitting on top of 寸 (a hand) that grabs at something. In its old form, the character showed a bird slipping free of a grasping hand. It's all about snatching and taking by force.
Picture something big 大 lifting off and flying away over the fields 田. That burst of upward effort is 奋: to rouse yourself and strive.
土 (earth) marks this as land: 境 is where a field's ground ends, its border, and by extension a region. 竟 on the right gives the sound jìng.
囗 (enclosure) wraps all the way around 卷, which gives the sound, so you get a closed circle or ring. In another reading the same enclosure is a pen where sheep are kept.
Embroidery is done with thread, so 纟 (silk) gives the meaning, and 秀 gives the sound xiù.
Rust eats away at metal, so 锈 has 钅 (metal) on the left for the meaning. 秀 (xiù) on the right gives the sound.
Three 人 (person) are stacked together, one on top and two below. As the English saying goes, three people make a crowd, so 众 means a crowd or the masses.
A hoof is an animal's foot, so 足 (foot) gives the meaning. 帝 (dì, ‘emperor’) gives the sound: tí.
Picture 土 (earth) heaped up into a mound. That's a pile. 隹 (short-tailed bird) is there for the sound, duī.
The 米 (rice) at the bottom marks 粱 as a grain, millet or sorghum, and 刅 on top gives the sound liáng. Don't confuse it with 梁, which has 木 (tree) at the bottom instead.
巨 began as a drawing of a carpenter's square with a handle. Imagine a builder gripping a huge square to lay out something big, and you have ‘large, great.’
矩 (carpenter's square, rule) is 巨 with 矢 ‘arrow’ added to make its meaning clear. 巨 also gives the sound, jǔ.
Picture one hand gripping two stalks of 禾 (grain) together. Holding both at once gives the meanings ‘both,’ ‘at the same time,’ and ‘to combine.’
欠 ‘lacking’ signals falling short, and 兼 gives the sound. When you've come up short you say sorry, and a harvest that comes up short is a crop failure.
Picture 贝 (cowrie shell, old money) sitting next to 兼 (to combine): you pile shells together, and that's how you earn a profit. 兼 also hints at the sound.
口 (mouth) tells you the meaning: something comes out of the mouth when you spit or vomit. 土 (tǔ) gives the sound.
⺼ (flesh, meat) tells you this is a body part, and 土 (tǔ) gives the sound dù. Your belly is the fleshy part of you.
A gorge is a narrow pass squeezed between mountains: 山 (mountain) gives the meaning, and 夹 ‘squeeze between’ suggests the pinched space and gives the sound xiá.
牛 (ox) gives the meaning of a farm or sacrificial animal, and 生 (shēng) gives the sound: an ox raised to be offered up.
氵 (water) sits next to 目 ‘eye’: water coming out of the eye means tears, or to cry.
麦 started out as a drawing of a wheat plant, so picture a stalk of wheat standing in the field whenever you see it.
Put 足 (foot) together with 失 (to lose) and you get losing your footing, so 跌 means to stumble and fall. Prices can fall this way too.
刂 (knife) splits things apart, and judging means separating right from wrong. 半 (bàn, ‘half’) gives the sound pàn.
吨 comes from the English word ‘ton.’ The 口 (mouth) tells you to say it for its sound, and 屯 (dūn) gives that sound.
不 ‘not’ sits on top of 正 ‘straight’. Something that is not straight is slanted, askew, or crooked.
不 ‘not’ sits on top of 用 ‘use’: if something is of no use, you don't need it. So 甭 means ‘don't bother’ or ‘no need to.’
Picture two items 口 threaded onto one vertical line 丨, like pieces of meat on a skewer. That's 串: to string things together, or a string of them.
Welding takes 火 (fire) for the meaning, and 旱 (hàn) gives the sound, so 焊 is also read hàn.
石 (rock, standing for minerals) plus 咸 ‘salty’ gives a salty mineral, which is alkali. 咸 (xián) also gives the sound jiǎn.
Picture a cave 穴 with pottery 缶 inside, fired until it hardens. That's a kiln. The 穴 on top tells you it's a hollow, dug-out place, which is also why the character can mean a pit or a coal mine.
A monkey 禺 sits on top of the 心 (heart-mind): think with a monkey's mind and you act stupid or foolish. 禺 also gives the sound yú.
Picture bringing a 石 (rock) down hard to smash something. 石 gives the meaning ‘to smash, pound,’ and 匝 hints at the sound zá.
Tiny bits of earth are dust: 小 (small) sits on top of 土 (earth), so 尘 means dust or dirt.
A hand 攵 (tapping with a stick) drives an ox 牛 ‘cow’ along, so the character means to herd cattle, or someone who does it: a shepherd.
